sections.heading: Programming and algorithms
paragraphs: Programming is the process of expressing a solution as instructions a computer can execute. A programming language provides symbols and rules (syntax) for communicating those instructions.

An algorithm is a finite, ordered and unambiguous sequence of steps for solving a problem. A useful algorithm is correct, clear, sufficiently efficient and independent of a particular programming language.

sections.heading: Computer organization and language generations
bullets: Input devices provide data; output devices present results; memory holds instructions and data; the CPU controls execution and includes the arithmetic and logic unit; secondary storage retains data and programs.

Machine language consists of machine-specific instructions. Assembly uses symbolic operation names and requires an assembler. High-level languages are more readable and need translation to machine code.

The course introduces language generations and the distinction between low-level, hardware-dependent languages and higher-level abstractions. Higher abstraction can improve readability while hiding some machine details.
Operating systems evolved from batch processing toward multiprogramming and time-sharing, allowing improved sharing of computer resources.

sections.heading: Programming paradigms and software development
bullets: Procedural programming organizes steps and procedure calls; structured programming builds programs from understandable blocks and limits unstructured jumps; object-oriented programming organizes behavior and data around interacting objects.
The software development life cycle includes investigation, analysis, design, implementation, testing and maintenance.
Top-down design breaks a large problem into smaller tasks; bottom-up design builds from lower-level components. Both help manage complexity.
A flowchart represents algorithm steps with standard symbols: terminal for start/end, parallelogram for input/output, rectangle for process, diamond for decision, and arrows for control flow.
A compiler translates source code as a whole into object or executable code; an interpreter translates and executes instructions incrementally. C++ commonly uses a compile-and-link workflow.

Typical program creation includes editing, preprocessing, compilation, linking, loading and execution. The preprocessor handles directives such as #include; the linker resolves external library references.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Distinguish algorithm, source program, compiler and executable.
Draw a flowchart for a decision or repetition problem and label the control flow.
Compare procedural, structured and object-oriented approaches.

sections.heading: Basic program structure
bullets: A C++ source file conventionally uses the .cpp extension. A program begins execution at main(). Standard modern form is int main() { ... return 0; }.
Preprocessor directives begin with #, such as #include <iostream>. Declarations introduce names and types; statements carry out operations; braces group a block; most statements end with a semicolon.
Use std::cout for output and std::cin for input with the stream operators << and >>. Include <iostream> and either qualify names with std:: or use a suitable using declaration.
Example: int age; std::cout << "Enter age: "; std::cin >> age; std::cout << "Age: " << age << '\n';
Comments // … and /* … */ are ignored by the compiler. Use them to explain intent, while descriptive names and indentation carry much of the code’s structure.

sections.heading: Variables, types and constants
bullets: A variable is a named memory location with a type that determines the kind of value it stores and the operations permitted. Common types include int, float, double, char and bool.
Choose types deliberately: integer types store whole numbers; floating-point types approximate real values; char stores a character; bool stores true or false.
Initialize variables before use. Uninitialized local variables do not have a reliable value.
Identifiers use letters, digits and underscores, cannot begin with a digit, and cannot be reserved keywords. C++ is case-sensitive.
A constant has a value that should not change. Use const for named constants; literals are values written directly in code.
Operators include arithmetic (+, −, *, /, %), assignment (=), comparison (==, !=, <, <=, >, >=), logical (&&, ||, !) and increment/decrement (++/--). Distinguish assignment = from equality ==.

sections.heading: Expressions, conversion and precedence
bullets: An expression combines values, variables and operators to produce a result. Parentheses make intended evaluation order explicit.
Integer division truncates the fractional part: 7/2 is 3 when both operands are integers. Use a floating operand, such as 7.0/2, when a fractional result is needed.
Type conversion may be implicit or explicit. Be careful when converting between integer and floating-point types because information can be lost.
The conditional operator condition ? value1 : value2 chooses one of two expressions based on a Boolean condition.

Increment and decrement change a variable by one. Prefix and postfix forms differ in whether the expression yields the updated or previous value; avoid complex expressions that obscure this difference.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Trace a short program by tracking each variable after every statement.
Predict integer division and operator precedence; add parentheses where ambiguity is possible.
Find syntax errors involving missing semicolons, braces, declarations or mismatched types.

sections.heading: Conditions and comparisons
bullets: A condition evaluates to true or false. Relational operators compare values; logical operators combine or negate conditions.
For &&, both conditions must be true; for ||, at least one must be true; ! reverses truth. Short-circuit evaluation may skip the right side when the result is already determined.

Use == to compare equality, not =. A common logic error is writing a condition that is always true, such as x < 0 || x > 10 when testing that x is outside the interval (which is appropriate only for that intended test).

sections.heading: if, if-else and nested decisions
bullets: An if statement executes a block only when its condition is true: if (condition) { statements; }.
if-else selects exactly one of two paths. An else-if chain checks alternatives in order; the first true branch executes.
Nested if statements put one decision inside another. Use braces and indentation to make the association between else and if unambiguous.
For several discrete alternatives based on one integral or enum expression, switch-case can improve clarity. Include break where fall-through is not intended and a default branch where appropriate.
The conditional operator is concise for a simple two-way value choice, but multi-step logic is clearer with if-else.

sections.heading: Designing reliable decisions
bullets: Test boundary values and mutually exclusive cases. For a range divided at 0 and 100, decide which branch includes each boundary.
Use && for a value inside a bounded interval (x >= low && x <= high); use || for outside it (x < low || x > high).
Avoid comparing floating-point calculations for exact equality when rounding may occur; use a tolerance when appropriate.
A decision table or flowchart can expose missing cases before coding.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Trace if/else-if code for true and false conditions and state which output occurs.
Rewrite a compound condition in words and check whether && or || matches the intended logic.
Develop a decision algorithm for parity, maximum of values, grading bands or sign classification.

sections.heading: while, do-while and for
bullets: A while loop tests its condition before each iteration and may execute zero times. Update loop state so the condition eventually becomes false.
A do-while loop executes its body at least once, then tests the condition; its syntax ends with a semicolon after while(condition).
A for loop groups initialization, continuation condition and update: for (initialization; condition; update). It suits count-controlled repetition.
Use while when repetition depends on a condition checked before work; do-while when at least one execution is required; for when a counter or sequence is natural.
A loop invariant is a statement that remains true before and after each iteration and can help reason about correctness.

sections.heading: Counters, accumulators and loop control
bullets: A counter tracks how many times something occurs; an accumulator combines values, often by initializing a sum to 0 or a product to 1 before looping.
A sentinel value signals the end of input and should generally not be included in the accumulated data.
break exits the nearest loop or switch; continue skips to the next iteration. Use them sparingly so control flow remains easy to follow.
Nested loops place one loop inside another. For each outer iteration, the inner loop typically completes its own sequence; count total operations by multiplying iteration counts when independent.
Off-by-one errors arise from incorrect start, end or comparison choices. Test zero, one, and boundary iteration counts.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Trace loop variables in a table for every iteration, including the final failed condition.
Write loops to compute sums, factorials, counts and simple patterns; initialize and update each variable correctly.
Explain whether a loop runs zero, one or many times and identify possible infinite-loop conditions.

sections.heading: Function design and calls
bullets: A function is a named unit of reusable code. A declaration/prototype specifies its name, return type and parameter types before use; a definition supplies the body.
A function call passes arguments to parameters. Return a value with return when the function’s return type is non-void; void functions perform work without returning a value.

Pass by value gives a function a copy, so changes to the parameter do not change the caller’s variable. Pass by reference (type&) allows the function to modify the original; const reference can avoid copying while preventing modification.
Break a problem into functions with focused responsibilities. Clear parameters and return values make code easier to test and reuse.

sections.heading: Scope and storage duration
bullets: Local variables are visible within their block; global variables are declared outside functions and are broadly accessible, but excessive global state makes programs harder to reason about.
A variable’s scope determines where its name is accessible. A block’s closing brace ends the scope of ordinary local declarations.
A static local variable retains its value between calls and is initialized once; this differs from an ordinary local variable created anew for each call.
Use meaningful names and avoid shadowing a variable from an outer scope unless there is a clear reason.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Trace a function call by recording argument values, parameter values and returned result.
Distinguish pass-by-value from pass-by-reference and determine whether the caller’s variable changes.
Identify local, global and static variables and explain their lifetime or visibility.

sections.heading: Arrays
bullets: An array stores a fixed-size sequence of elements of the same type. Elements are indexed from 0 through size−1; accessing outside that range is an error and can cause undefined behavior.
Declare and initialize arrays with a type and size or an initializer list. Use loops to process elements and keep the index condition within bounds.
For a two-dimensional array, use row and column indices; nested loops naturally traverse rows and columns.

When an array is passed to a function in traditional C++, it decays to a pointer to its first element, so pass the length separately or use a safer container such as std::array or std::vector in modern C++.

sections.heading: Character arrays and strings
bullets: A C-style string is a character array ending in the null character '\0'. Its storage must include space for the terminator.
The C string library provides operations such as strlen for length, strcpy for copying and strcat for concatenation; destination capacity must be sufficient to avoid buffer overflow.
In modern C++, std::string from <string> is safer and easier for ordinary text operations. Use getline when a full line including spaces is needed.
Input with >> stops at whitespace; getline reads through the line ending. If mixing formatted extraction with getline, handle the leftover newline deliberately.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Determine array indices and trace a traversal loop without stepping beyond the last element.
Distinguish a character from a string and explain the null terminator in C-style strings.
Choose between token input and line input based on whether spaces are part of the data.

sections.heading: Pointer fundamentals
bullets: Each object occupies memory with an address. A pointer variable stores an address of an object of a compatible type.
The address-of operator & obtains an object’s address; the dereference operator * accesses the object at a pointer’s address.
Example: int value=15; int* ptr=&value; *ptr=20; changes value to 20. The pointer itself holds an address, while *ptr refers to the pointed-to value.
Initialize pointers before use. nullptr represents a pointer that intentionally points to no object; dereferencing nullptr or an invalid/dangling pointer is undefined behavior.
Pointer arithmetic advances by elements of the pointed-to type, not raw bytes. It is only valid within an array and one past its end (without dereferencing that one-past position).

sections.heading: Pointers, arrays and function parameters
bullets: An array name often converts to a pointer to its first element in expressions; indexing a[i] is equivalent to *(a+i) within valid bounds.
A pointer can be passed to a function to allow indirect access to data, but specify whether null is allowed and ensure the pointed object remains alive.
A pointer to pointer stores the address of another pointer. Each dereference level follows one address; count * operators carefully.
Const placement changes what may be modified: const int* prevents modifying the pointed integer through that pointer; int* const prevents changing the pointer’s stored address.

sections.heading: Dynamic memory and safe use
bullets: In older C++ material, new allocates an object or array and delete/delete[] releases it. Every allocation must be released exactly once with the matching form.
Common errors include memory leaks (not releasing owned memory), double deletion, use-after-free, dangling pointers and out-of-bounds access.
Modern C++ generally prefers automatic objects and standard containers such as std::vector, or smart pointers, which manage resource lifetime more safely.
Ownership should be clear: know which part of a program is responsible for releasing dynamically allocated resources.

sections.heading: Exam quick check
bullets: Trace pointer values separately from the values they point to.
Explain the difference between ptr, *ptr and &variable.
Identify whether a snippet risks a null dereference, out-of-bounds access, leak or dangling pointer.

topics.title: Text files, streams and error handling

sections.heading: File streams
bullets: The <fstream> library provides file stream types: ifstream for reading, ofstream for writing and fstream for both. Associate a stream with a filename using a constructor or open().
Check that a file opened successfully before reading or writing. A failed open may result from a missing file, path error or permission issue.
Read formatted values with >>, a whole line with getline, and write using <<. Select append mode when existing contents should be retained; ordinary output may truncate an existing file.
Close a file when finished, although stream destructors also close resources automatically. Check stream state to detect end-of-file or I/O errors.

sections.heading: Reliable file processing
bullets: Prefer reading in a loop that tests the extraction operation, such as while (infile >> value), rather than testing eof() before the read; this avoids processing stale data after a failed extraction.
Validate data as it is read and handle malformed or missing input explicitly. Use clear error messages and return or recover appropriately.
Keep filenames, open modes and stream lifetimes clear. Separate file parsing from calculations and output when programs grow.
A program that works with keyboard input can often be adapted to files by replacing cin/cout with input and output file streams.

sections.heading: Final exam review
bullets: Write the main stages of program development and explain how algorithms and flowcharts support implementation.
Trace code involving data types, expressions, decisions, loops, functions, arrays and pointers.
Select the right control structure and produce a short readable C++ solution with initialization, valid bounds and clear output.
Explain how to open, process, validate and close a file, including what to do when opening or reading fails.
